Maladaptive Strategies.value: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event
Going out at night or being outside after dark
Paying attention to or looking at my own body

Threat.value: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening

issues.explanation: The trigger set is not clinically coherent for a single assault presentation as described. 'Shouting in Arabic' implies a very specific perpetrator/context cue, while 'fire or flames' suggests a qualitatively different trauma context that is not supported by the memory, appraisal, threat, or strategy items. This is hard to reconcile as one assault-based PTSD profile rather than merely heterogeneous triggers.

The threat item about monitoring for someone entering the home is weakly connected to the rest of the profile. Other threat items center on being followed and re-experiencing the assault, while the triggers and strategies point to external assault cues and body-related avoidance rather than a home-intrusion scenario. This makes the home-entry threat concern look like a mismatched threat context within the profile.

vignette:
# Jasmine's Story

Jasmine was nineteen when she married Marcus, a decision that had felt like the right one at the time—a commitment to someone who made her feel seen. She had been working part-time at a coffee shop near campus, saving money, imagining a future that felt manageable and warm. That was before the night in October when everything fractured into something unrecognizable.

She had been walking home from a late shift, cutting through the parking garage as she always did. A man had been waiting. She had not seen his face clearly in the darkness, but she heard his voice—sharp, commanding, in Arabic, a language she did not understand but that seemed to carry a violence of its own. He had smelled of alcohol, thick and suffocating. There had been the sound of his motorcycle outside the garage afterward, the engine roaring as he fled, a sound that had etched itself into her nervous system with such precision that months later, any motorcycle in the distance would send her body into a state of alert that felt like drowning while standing still.

In the weeks that followed, Jasmine had tried to return to work. But the coffee shop, with its open layout and glass doors, had begun to feel indefensible. She found herself listening constantly for sounds—the scrape of a chair, the jingle of keys—interpreting each one as a potential threat. One afternoon, a customer had shouted in Arabic to his friend across the café, and Jasmine had frozen, her hands shaking so badly that she dropped an entire tray of cups. She had not returned after that shift. Marcus had said it was okay, that he could support them both, but the loss of that small independence had added another weight to the ones already pressing down on her chest.

The nights became impossible. She could not bring herself to go outside after dark. The thought of being in the open, where someone could approach from behind, made her skin crawl. She had taken to checking behind her constantly, even in their apartment, even in rooms she had just looked at moments before. The checking never brought relief, only a temporary pause before the fear crept back in. Marcus had noticed her doing it—spinning around, peering into shadows—and she could see the worry in his eyes, the unspoken question about whether she was becoming someone he did not recognize. She was becoming someone she did not recognize.

Certain dates had become unbearable. The anniversary of the assault approached like a storm she could see on the horizon, and the dread began weeks in advance. She had started avoiding that entire week in October, staying in bed, refusing to engage with the world. The smell of alcohol—on Marcus's breath after he came home from seeing friends, in the air at a grocery store—would send her spiraling backward into that garage, the sensations returning with a vividness that made her question whether she was remembering or reliving.

What frightened her most was not just the fear itself, but what she had come to believe about herself. She had once been someone who worked, who moved through the world with a kind of confidence that now felt like a fantasy she had invented. She found herself unable to look at her own body without feeling a deep revulsion, as though her skin had become a thing that had betrayed her. She would shower with her eyes closed, dress without mirrors. When she thought about what had happened, she did not just see it—she heard the Arabic words again, smelled the alcohol, felt the weight of a hand she could not escape. The memories arrived without warning, triggered by the smallest sensory echo, and she had no defense against them.

What haunted her most, though, was the conviction that someone else—someone braver, someone stronger—would have fought back, would have stopped it from happening. The world, she had come to believe, was not a place where safety existed. It was a place where violence waited in parking garages and in the voices of strangers, and she was not capable of surviving it the way other people might.

It was Marcus who finally insisted she see someone. He had found her one morning sitting on the bathroom floor, unable to move, and something in his face—fear mixed with helplessness—had broken through her isolation enough to make her agree. She had called a therapist that afternoon, her hands trembling as she dialed, terrified of what it would mean to speak it all aloud, but more terrified of the alternative: a life spent checking behind her, avoiding her own body, waiting for the next sound that would send her back to that garage.
